cards.say: Most AI decisions aren't "should we use AI". They're **build it, buy a product, or bring in a partner**. Each trades speed, cost and control differently.

cards.q: Match each option to its main trade-off
pairs: Fast to start, less control over the details
Most control, slowest and most expensive
A middle ground: some customization, shared risk
cards.why: None of these is always right. The best fit depends on how unique your need is and how much upkeep you can commit to.

cards.q: Which situation usually favors buying instead of building?
options: The task is common across many companies, like scheduling or transcription
The task depends entirely on data only your company has
You want to fully control the model's behavior forever
cards.why: If many companies need the same thing, someone has likely already built and refined it. Building it yourself there mostly means re-inventing it, slower.

cards.q: Which situation usually favors building in-house?
options: The workflow is core to your edge and hard to buy off the shelf
You want something running by next week
Nobody on the team has time to maintain it
cards.why: Build where it's central to your advantage and worth the ongoing investment. Buy where it isn't.

cards.q: One of these vendor-evaluation habits is weak. Tap it.
sentences: Ask how the vendor handles your data and who can see it.
Pick whichever product's website lists the most features.
Ask what happens to your workflow if you switch vendors later.
cards.why: A long feature list doesn't tell you whether it solves your actual problem. Ask about your specific use case, and about the exit.

cards.q: Put a sound evaluation process in order
steps: Define what the task actually needs to do
Compare build, buy and partner options against that
Run a small pilot with real data
Decide, based on the pilot's results
cards.why: Define the need first, or every option looks equally appealing.
